At the playground in Berlin, Vera squirmed beside the swing, hopping from foot to foot while a bigger boy swung and swung. She reached for the chain.
"Not yet," said her father Felix, kneeling beside her. "Let's count his swings. Ten more, then it's yours."
"One, two..." Vera counted loudly, holding her own elbows to keep her hands still. By seven she was singing the numbers. When the boy hopped off she clapped and climbed on.
"That was a long wait," said Felix.
Vera nodded, pumping her legs.

qa.q: What did Felix and Vera count while they waited?
qa.a: They counted the bigger boy's swings.

qa.q: What is Vera feeling as she squirms beside the swing?
qa.a: Impatient and eager. She hops from foot to foot, reaches for the chain and has to hold her own elbows to keep her hands still.

qa.q: What choice by Felix helped Vera wait?
qa.a: He knelt beside her and turned the wait into a count, promising it was hers after ten more swings.

qa.q: How might the bigger boy feel with Vera waiting beside the swing?
qa.a: Perhaps a little watched, but Vera's counting shows the wait is fair and short, so he can finish his turn.

grounding: A child squirms and grabs while waiting for a swing, and counting makes the short wait bearable.

Yusuf had forty rupees in his tin, and the shop window held a remote-control car that cost four hundred. Every Sunday he stood in front of it. His friends bought sweets and sticker packets. Yusuf's fingers twitched near a pack of cricket cards.
"Buy it, beta, it's your money," said his mother Binita.
"I'll wait," said Yusuf.
"Next month?"
"Maybe two."
At home he drew ten squares on a sheet of paper and coloured one in each time he added coins. Binita had told him the shopkeeper would keep the car aside for him, and every Sunday the shopkeeper nodded at the window.
Three months later Yusuf carried the box home, and it felt heavier and better than any sweet.

qa.q: How many rupees did Yusuf have in his tin at the start?
qa.a: Forty rupees.

qa.q: What is Yusuf feeling as he stands at the shop window and passes the cricket cards?
qa.a: He is tempted but determined. His fingers twitch near the cards, yet he says he will wait for the car.

qa.q: What choice helped Yusuf keep saving?
qa.a: He drew ten squares and coloured one each time he added coins, so his progress was visible, and he trusted that the shopkeeper would keep the car aside.

qa.q: How might Binita feel watching Yusuf choose to wait?
qa.a: Probably proud and a little amazed, since she says it is his money but he decides to wait.

grounding: A child saves pocket money for a bigger toy instead of spending it, trusting the reward will arrive.

Our teacher walked over to Jomon and didn't sigh. She drew the sum as a chocolate bar and waited while he tried. When Jomon got it, she just nodded, as if it hadn't taken long at all.

In the hostel common room, Sumit slammed his diary shut. "Two more years of this!" he told Vikas Sir, the warden, who was stacking chairs. "Curfew, a fixed timetable, asking permission to go to the market. I want to run my own life now and be somebody."
Vikas Sir did not lecture. "That sounds like a long road," he said. "What's one thing you could own this month?"
Sumit scowled, then muttered, "Planning the Diwali fund for the hostel."
"Good. Bring me a plan by Friday."
Sumit stomped off. On Friday he came back with a page of figures, and for the first time the two years looked like a set of smaller steps.

qa.a: Two more years.

qa.q: What is Sumit feeling as he slams his diary shut?
qa.a: Frustrated and impatient. He resents the curfew and permissions and wants to run his own life now.

qa.a: He treats it as a real feeling of a long wait and does not lecture, instead offering a concrete task that gives Sumit some ownership.

Dear Imran Bhai,
You asked how school is. Honestly? It feels like waiting in a queue that never moves. At home everyone still treats me like a kid: no phone after nine, no travelling alone, no say in what I study. You left home at eighteen, and I want that now, not in three years.
I have started crossing off days on a calendar, which is silly, I know. Last week Papa let me plan the route for our family trip, and for three days I felt grown. Maybe the small yeses are the road.

Nirmala

qa.a: Probably fond and understanding, since Imran left home at eighteen and Nirmala looks up to Imran enough to ask if the wait goes faster.

In the small-town market, Kishore had watched his neighbour Gautam wait eleven months for his cousin Anil to apologise over a broken shop agreement. "I'm being patient," Gautam said whenever the name came up. Every festival he laid an extra plate for Anil, and every festival it stayed empty. He began taking the long way to avoid Anil's shop.
Kishore noticed Gautam's tight jaw and that he had never once said, "That hurt me."
One evening over tea Kishore said, "Patience has a limit. Is it patience if you're avoiding the conversation?"
Gautam stared at his glass. "I'm scared Anil will say no."
"Then at least you'd know," said Kishore.
Gautam nodded slowly. "Sunday," he said.

qa.q: How many months has Gautam waited for the apology?
qa.a: Eleven months.

qa.q: What is Kishore feeling and thinking about Gautam's waiting?
qa.a: Kishore is worried and honest. Kishore notices the tight jaw and the avoidance and suspects the patience is really avoiding the conversation.

qa.q: What turning point did Kishore's question bring?
qa.a: Kishore asked whether it was patience if Gautam was avoiding the conversation, and Gautam admitted fear and decided to go on Sunday.

qa.q: What might Gautam be afraid of?
qa.a: Gautam is afraid that Anil will say no, which is why he has waited instead of asking.

grounding: A person waits for an apology, calling it patience, while avoiding a needed conversation.

Lucia had won the regional robotics prize, and when her classmates in Osaka cheered she laughed it off. "It was luck. Anyone could have built it." At home she hid the medal in a drawer and told her cousin the design was mostly the team's, though she had written most of the code.
